The problem

A reference is a value that lets code reach an object. Two variables refer to the same bookmark counter. A helper receives one of them. Can it change what the other variable reads?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

Each variable holds a reference. The call copies that value into the helper frame. Writing eight into the object changes the field visible through both names. Reassigning the helper parameter to a newly created counter changes only the local copy. Reverse the two statements in edit. Now the write lands on the new object and both caller variables still see seven. Compare the order of the field write and local store in the disassembly.

Call the original object A and the new one B. These letters label their identity so we can follow each object even when two objects happen to store the same number. A field belongs to an object. A parameter is a local name initialized when the call starts.

Counter first = new Counter(7);
Counter second = first;
edit(second);
Operation inside the examplefirstsecondinsideField values
Enter editAAAA holds 7
Write inside.value = 8AAAA holds 8
Assign inside = new Counter(99)AABA holds 8, B holds 99
Return to callerAAhelper finishedcaller reads 8 twice

Suppose the caller wants second to refer to B after the call. Have the helper return B, then assign that returned value to second in the caller. First continues to refer to A. This explains how one method can change a shared object's contents while replacing a caller's variable requires a separate assignment.

Check yourself

Reassign the parameter before writing eight. Which value does first see?

Not quite. The caller still points at the original object. Re-read that part ↑

Right. A copied reference can still point to the same object. Reassigning one local changes only that local.

The helper writes eight, creates B and returns B. The caller ignores the result. Which object does second reach?

Not quite. Returning a value does not assign it to second. Re-read that part ↑

Right. The caller still holds the copied reference to A.

The caller assigns returned B to second. What does first reach?

Right. Track the two names independently, even when they originally held the same value.

Not quite. The assignment changed just the caller's second variable. Re-read that part ↑

Sources
  • Java language specification, method invocation — “assign the argument values to corresponding freshly created parameter variables”

What you now know

A copied reference can still point to the same object. Reassigning one local changes only that local.
